course_title: Google IT Automation with Python Professional Certificate
chapter_summary:
Automating communication is a cornerstone of effective IT automation. Whether it's sending system alerts, daily reports, or task completion notifications, Python provides robust tools to handle email and integrate with various messaging platforms. This chapter will equip you with the skills to make your scripts proactive, keeping you and your team informed.

At the heart of sending emails is the SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol). Python's `smtplib` module provides a client interface to the SMTP protocol, allowing your scripts to connect to an SMTP server (like Gmail's, Outlook's, or your organization's internal server) and send emails. The basic workflow involves creating an `SMTP_SSL` object (for secure connections), logging in with your credentials, and then using the `send_message()` method. It's crucial to use `SMTP_SSL` or `starttls()` for encrypted communication to protect your credentials and email content during transit. When logging in, you'll need the SMTP server address (e.g., `smtp.gmail.com`), the port (typically 465 for SSL or 587 for TLS), your email address, and an application-specific password or token, not your main account password, especially for services like Gmail. Hardcoding passwords directly into scripts is a major security risk; always use environment variables or a secure configuration management system to store sensitive information.

While `smtplib` handles the sending mechanism, the `email` package (specifically `email.mime`) is responsible for constructing the email message itself. For simple plain-text emails, you can directly pass a string to `send_message()`. However, for more sophisticated emails with subjects, multiple recipients, HTML content, or attachments, you'll use objects like `MIMEText` for text/HTML bodies and `MIMEMultipart` to combine different parts (text, HTML, attachments) into a single message. `MIMEApplication` or `MIMEBase` are used for adding attachments. Constructing a `MIMEMultipart` message involves setting `From`, `To`, and `Subject` headers, creating `MIMEText` parts for plain text and HTML versions (for better compatibility across email clients), and then attaching files. Providing both plain-text and HTML versions of an email is a best practice, as some email clients might not render HTML, or users might prefer plain text.

Beyond traditional email, many organizations rely on chat platforms like Slack, Microsoft Teams, or Discord for real-time communication. Python scripts can easily integrate with these services using webhooks. A webhook is a user-defined HTTP callback that is triggered by an event. For platforms like Slack, you can configure an incoming webhook URL. Your Python script then simply makes an HTTP `POST` request to this URL with a JSON payload containing the message text and other formatting options. This approach is often simpler and faster for immediate notifications than sending an email, especially for internal team alerts. The `requests` library, which we covered in the previous chapter, is perfect for this task. Remember to keep webhook URLs secure, as anyone with the URL can post messages to your channel.

Common mistakes when automating emails include not using secure connections (SSL/TLS), hardcoding credentials, or not handling potential SMTP authentication failures. For attachments, ensure you open the file in binary read mode (`'rb'`) and correctly set the MIME type. When sending notifications, always consider the audience and frequency. Over-notifying can lead to alert fatigue, where important messages get ignored. Design your automation to send concise, actionable information only when necessary. By combining `smtplib`, the `email` package, and the `requests` library for webhooks, your Python automation scripts can become powerful communicators, ensuring critical information reaches the right people at the right time.

screens.title: Automating Email and Notifications
screens.subtitle: Use Python to send emails, attach reports, and post notifications safely

narration.text: In this chapter you will learn how to make your automation talk back to people. We focus on sending email programmatically with the SMTP protocol and constructing messages with Python's built-in email package. You'll see secure connection patterns like using SMTP_SSL or starttls, how to build plain-text and H T M L alternatives with MIMEMultipart and MIMEText, and how to attach files safely by opening them in binary mode. We also cover lightweight integrations using webhooks for chat platforms, where a single HTTP POST delivers a notification to a channel. Practical security matters a lot: do not hardcode credentials, prefer environment variables or application-specific passwords, and ensure SSL/TLS is used. Through an end-to-end activity you'll generate a daily report, attach it to an email and simulate a Slack notification. By the end, you should be able to send a tested, secure automated message and know common pitfalls to avoid. Consider which notifications your team actually needs before automating them.

screens.title: What is SMTP and how smtplib fits in
screens.subtitle: Understand the protocol that moves mail and the Python client that speaks it

narration.text: SMTP stands for Simple Mail Transfer Protocol and it is the standard for sending email between machines. It defines commands and replies used to hand off a message from a sending client to a mail server and then between servers until delivery. In Python, the smtplib module implements an SMTP client you can control in a script. You create an SMTP or SMTP_SSL object, provide the server address and port, authenticate, and then send. Use SMTP_SSL when the server accepts an SSL-wrapped connection on a port like 465; use starttls to upgrade an unencrypted connection, usually on port 587. A concrete example: connecting to smtp. gmail. com with SMTP_SSL and logging in using an application-specific password lets you send mail without web automation. A common misconception is that sending email is just writing a message and calling send; in reality you must set headers correctly and handle server responses and failures. Key takeaway: SMTP is a conversation between client and server; smtplib gives your script the voice to participate, but you must manage secure transport and authentication. What is SMTP and how smtplib fits in means smtp is the protocol; smtplib is python's client implementation used to connect, authenticate, and send messages over smtp.. In practical terms, understand the protocol that moves mail and the python client that speaks it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: SMTP + smtplib

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › SMTP Basics
Definition

SMTP is the protocol used to submit and transfer email messages. smtplib is the Python module that opens a network connection, authenticates, and issues SMTP commands to send a message programmatically.

Quick bullets
  • Use SMTP_SSL for an SSL-wrapped connection.
  • Use starttls() to upgrade a plain connection to TLS.
  • Need server address, port, email, and a password or token.
Key Takeaway

SMTP is the transport; smtplib is your script's client. Always choose encrypted transport before authenticating.

Concrete Example
import smtplib
server = smtplib.SMTP_SSL('smtp.gmail.com', 465)
server.login('your_email@example.com', 'APP_PASSWORD')
# later: server.send_message(msg)
server.quit()
Misconception: using a regular account password is discouraged. Prefer an application-specific password or token for automated access.

screens.title: Securely connecting to an SMTP server
screens.subtitle: Choose SMTP_SSL or starttls and manage credentials safely

narration.text: Connecting securely is the first defense when your script sends email. There are two common patterns: an SSL-wrapped socket and an opportunistic upgrade. With SMTP_SSL you immediately open an encrypted channel to the server and then authenticate, which is straightforward when the server expects an SSL connection on a port like 465. The alternative is to open a plain SMTP connection on a port like 587 and call starttls() to upgrade to TLS before sending credentials. Both protect credentials in transit; which to use depends on the server's supported ports. Credentials themselves should avoid hardcoding. Store passwords in environment variables or use a secure configuration tool. In a local test, set an environment variable and read it from os. environ. For services like Gmail, use an application-specific password that you can revoke. Also handle exceptions: catch SMTPAuthenticationError and network errors, and log useful diagnostics without printing secrets. Reflection: if a server rejects TLS, do not fall back to unencrypted authentication—treat that as a configuration issue that must be fixed. Securely connecting to an SMTP server means prefer smtp_ssl or starttls() before authenticating, and keep credentials out of code using environment variables or tokens.. In practical terms, choose smtp_ssl or starttls and manage credentials safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Secure Connection Pattern
keyIdea.text: Prefer SMTP_SSL or starttls() before authenticating, and keep credentials out of code using environment variables or tokens.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Secure Connection
Connection Steps
1. Decide port and mode: 465 for SSL, 587 for starttls.
2. If using starttls, call starttls() before login.
3. Read credentials from environment variables.
4. Catch authentication and network errors and avoid revealing secrets in logs.
Code Snippet
import os
import smtplib
from smtplib import SMTP_SSL

password = os.environ.get('EMAIL_APP_PASSWORD')
server = SMTP_SSL('smtp.gmail.com', 465)
server.login('your_email@example.com', password)
# send messages
server.quit()
Open credentials via environment variables and avoid printing them. If login fails, check the port and whether an app-specific password is required.

screens.subtitle: Build and send a minimal message using smtplib

narration.text: A plain-text email is the simplest automation output and a good first test. The required pieces are From, To, and Subject headers plus a body. Closing question: when would a plain-text message be preferable to H T M L? Consider accessibility and simplicity. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Plain-text Email
Example Code
from email.mime.text import MIMEText
import smtplib

msg = MIMEText('Daily system status: all checks passed')
msg['Subject'] = 'Daily Report'
msg['From'] = 'monitor@example.com'
msg['To'] = 'admin@example.com'

with smtplib.SMTP_SSL('smtp.gmail.com', 465) as server:
  server.login('monitor@example.com', 'APP_PASSWORD')
  server.send_message(msg)
Bullets
  • Use MIMEText for clear text body content.
  • Set Subject, From, and To headers explicitly.
  • Use context managers to ensure server.quit() runs.
Key Takeaway

Start with plain-text emails for reliability and testability before adding HTML and attachments.

screens.title: Multipart messages: MIMEText and MIMEMultipart
screens.subtitle: Provide both plain-text and HTML parts so mail clients render the best option

narration.text: Multipart messages let you include alternate representations of the same content and attachments. The MIMEMultipart class acts as a container for multiple parts. When you provide both a plain-text and an H T M L version, initialize the MIMEMultipart with a subtype of alternative. Then create two MIMEText parts: one with subtype 'plain' and one with subtype 'html', and attach them in that order so clients pick the H T M L version when capable. For attachments, use a different multipart subtype, such as mixed, and attach the alternative part alongside file parts. A concrete example: a daily report can include a simple plain-text summary and a formatted H T M L table for richer clients. A common mistake is to send only H T M L, which will be unreadable to text-only clients or some automated processors. Key practice: always include a plain-text fallback and set From, To, and Subject on the top-level message so headers apply to all parts. Multipart messages: MIMEText and MIMEMultipart means use mimemultipart('alternative') for text/html pairs and mimemultipart('mixed') to combine alternatives with attachments.. In practical terms, provide both plain-text and html parts so mail clients render the best option. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Multipart Strategy
keyIdea.text: Use MIMEMultipart('alternative') for text/HTML pairs and MIMEMultipart('mixed') to combine alternatives with attachments.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Multipart Messages
What to include
  • Plain-text part for basic clients.
  • HTML part for richer formatting.
  • Attachments added as separate MIME parts with appropriate Content-Disposition.
Order matters: attach the plain-text first, then HTML, so clients can choose the best option.
Analogy
Think of MIMEMultipart as an envelope containing multiple formats of the same letter and files tucked inside. Recipients pick the format their mail reader understands.
Key Takeaway

Provide both plain and HTML alternatives, and attach files as separate MIME parts opened in binary mode.

screens.title: Attaching files safely using MIMEApplication
screens.subtitle: Open files in binary mode and set Content-Disposition to attachment

narration.text: Attachments extend the utility of automated emails by delivering logs, reports, and archives. When attaching a file, open it in binary mode using 'rb' to avoid corruption, and create a MIMEApplication or MIMEBase part with the file contents. Set headers on the attachment: include Content-Disposition as attachment with the filename so mail clients present it correctly. For example, open daily_report. txt in binary mode, create a MIMEApplication from its bytes, and attach it to a MIMEMultipart message. Remember to set the correct MIME type when known; for generic binary data, MIMEApplication is appropriate. A frequent mistake is opening files in text mode, which can change line endings or encoding unexpectedly. Also be mindful of file size limits imposed by SMTP servers; split or compress large attachments before sending. Finally, verify the attachment after sending by downloading it from the test mailbox and opening it locally to confirm integrity. Attaching files safely using MIMEApplication means open files with 'rb', wrap bytes in mimeapplication, set content-disposition to attachment, and verify attachments in tests.. In practical terms, open files in binary mode and set content-disposition to attachment. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Attachment Best Practices
keyIdea.text: Open files with 'rb', wrap bytes in MIMEApplication, set Content-Disposition to attachment, and verify attachments in tests.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Attachments
Attachment Example
from email.mime.application import MIMEApplication
from email.mime.multipart import MIMEMultipart

msg = MIMEMultipart()
msg['Subject'] = 'Daily Report'

with open('daily_report.txt', 'rb') as f:
  part = MIMEApplication(f.read(), Name='daily_report.txt')
  part['Content-Disposition'] = 'attachment; filename="daily_report.txt"'
  msg.attach(part)
Common Mistake
Opening binary files in text mode can corrupt attachments, especially across platforms. Always use 'rb'.
Key Takeaway

Attach files as MIME parts from binary reads and verify delivery in a test inbox.

screens.title: Live coding: build a MIMEMultipart email with HTML and attachment
screens.subtitle: Step through constructing alternatives and attaching a file

narration.text: In this live demo we build a complete MIMEMultipart message that includes a plain-text summary, an H T M L version, and a binary attachment. Start by creating a top-level MIMEMultipart with subtype mixed if you will include attachments. Then create an alternative part to hold the plain and H T M L representations. Attach the plain text first, then H T M L inside the alternative container, and finally attach the binary file. Authenticate to the SMTP server using SMTP_SSL or starttls and send the message with send_message. A concrete example helps: imagine a script that composes a status summary as plain text and an H T M L table. The H T M L makes it easy to scan, while the text ensures compatibility. Misconception to avoid: mixing subtypes incorrectly can cause attachments to be hidden or the H T M L to be ignored. After sending, check the inbox and the downloaded attachment to ensure both parts rendered and the file opens locally. Consider adding logging to capture server responses if delivery fails. Live coding: build a MIMEMultipart email with HTML and attachment means assemble alternative parts inside a mixed container, attach files last, and send over a secure connection while logging responses.. In practical terms, step through constructing alternatives and attaching a file. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Live Coding Demo
Complete Example
from email.mime.multipart import MIMEMultipart
from email.mime.text import MIMEText
from email.mime.application import MIMEApplication
import smtplib
import os

msg = MIMEMultipart('mixed')
msg['Subject'] = 'Daily Report'
msg['From'] = 'monitor@example.com'
msg['To'] = 'admin@example.com'

alt = MIMEMultipart('alternative')
alt.attach(MIMEText('Text summary of the report','plain'))
alt.attach(MIMEText('
Report
All checks OK
','html'))
msg.attach(alt)

with open('daily_report.txt','rb') as f:
  part = MIMEApplication(f.read(), Name='daily_report.txt')
  part['Content-Disposition'] = 'attachment; filename="daily_report.txt"'
  msg.attach(part)

with smtplib.SMTP_SSL('smtp.gmail.com',465) as server:
  server.login('monitor@example.com', os.environ.get('EMAIL_APP_PASSWORD'))
  server.send_message(msg)
Checkpoints
  • Alternative parts first, attachments last.
  • Open attachments in 'rb' and set filename in Content-Disposition.
  • Read credentials from environment variables.
Key Takeaway

Follow the composition order and secure credentials; verify the message and attachment in a test inbox.

screens.title: Webhooks: sending chat notifications with requests
screens.subtitle: Use an HTTP POST to deliver quick notifications to a channel

narration.text: Webhooks are simple HTTP endpoints that accept POST requests to deliver messages into chat systems like Slack. Instead of sending an email, a script can post a small JSON payload to a webhook URL to notify a team immediately. Use the requests library to perform the POST with a JSON body containing a concise summary. Keep the webhook URL secret because anyone with that URL can post messages. For our exercise, simulate a webhook by defining a dummy URL and printing the requests. post response. A practical payload contains a short text like 'Daily system report generated and sent. Check your inbox!' and optional fields for formatting. A common misconception is that webhooks replace email entirely; they complement email by providing immediate, short notifications while attachments and formal records still belong in email. When using webhooks, consider rate limits and avoid alert fatigue by sending only actionable messages. Webhooks: sending chat notifications with requests means send concise json via requests.post to a secured webhook url for fast channel notifications; treat the url like a secret.. In practical terms, use an http post to deliver quick notifications to a channel. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Webhooks
Example Payload
import requests
import json

payload = {"text": "Daily system report generated and sent. Check your inbox!"}
response = requests.post('https://hooks.example/dummy', json=payload)
print(response.status_code, response.text)
Practical Notes
  • Treat webhook URLs like credentials and store them securely.
  • Keep messages short and actionable to avoid alert fatigue.
  • Simulate with a dummy URL during local testing and print the response.
Key Takeaway

Webhooks are a fast channel for short notifications; use JSON POSTs with requests and secure the webhook URL.

screens.title: Errors, retries, and alert fatigue
screens.subtitle: Handle SMTP failures and avoid overwhelming recipients

narration.text: When automating notifications, expect failures and design recovery paths. Common SMTP errors include authentication failures, network timeouts, or server rejections due to size or rate limits. Handle these by catching specific exceptions like SMTPAuthenticationError and SMTPRecipientsRefused, log the error details without exposing credentials, and implement retries with exponential backoff for transient network issues. Another class of problem is alert fatigue: scripts that notify too often cause people to ignore messages. Limit notifications to actionable events, consolidate repetitive messages into digests, or use severity thresholds. A typical pattern is to send an email with full detail and a short webhook summary for immediate awareness; ensure webhook messages are concise and infrequent. Misconception: automatic retries should be infinite; instead, cap retry attempts and escalate to a human if needed. Final reflection: design notifications so that recipients can act on them quickly, and instrument your automation to report its own health without causing noise. Errors, retries, and alert fatigue means implement targeted retries for transient errors, log safely, cap notifications to prevent alert fatigue, and escalate appropriately.. In practical terms, handle smtp failures and avoid overwhelming recipients. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Robust Notifications
keyIdea.text: Implement targeted retries for transient errors, log safely, cap notifications to prevent alert fatigue, and escalate appropriately.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Errors & Fatigue
Error Handling Checklist
  • Catch SMTPAuthenticationError and log without secrets.
  • Retry transient failures with exponential backoff and a cap.
  • Handle recipient refusals and size limit rejections gracefully.
Avoid Alert Fatigue
Send only necessary notifications. Aggregate frequent events and use severity levels to reduce noise.
Common Mistake

Sending too many low-value alerts reduces trust. Prioritize actionable messages and provide context for rapid action.

narration.text: Testing notification code safely is essential. Use sandbox mailboxes or disposable test accounts to receive messages without involving real recipients. For webhooks, define a dummy URL and print or log the requests. post response rather than posting to a production channel. Replace real application passwords with placeholders or environment variables during development and consider using local SMTP test servers or services that accept messages without relaying them to the Internet. When you must test with a real provider, restrict the recipient list to test accounts and generate an application-specific password that can be revoked. Verify attachments by downloading and opening them; check both plain-text and H T M L renderings. Also test error paths by intentionally failing authentication or sending an oversized attachment to observe your script's fallbacks. Misconception: unit tests that mock network calls are sufficient; they are important, but run integration tests against a safe sandbox as the final check before deployment. narration.text: These are the compact concepts you should recall when automating messages. SMTP is the protocol for sending mail; smtplib is the Python module that implements an SMTP client. The email package provides MIME classes like MIMEText for content and MIMEMultipart for building messages with multiple parts. MIMEApplication is used to include binary attachments. screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three quick concept cards and a final takeaway

narration.text: Keep three practical rules in mind as you implement automation. First, always secure transport: use SMTP_SSL or starttls before sending credentials to protect them in transit. Second, construct messages for compatibility: include both plain-text and H T M L parts and attach files opened in binary mode so clients can render or download content correctly. Third, protect secrets and avoid alert fatigue: store credentials outside code using environment variables or application-specific passwords, and design your notifications to be concise and actionable. These rules reduce risk and improve the usefulness of your automated messages. Before you finish, reflect: which notifications are essential and which can be consolidated into a digest to reduce noise?
